analysis.one_liner: Lets workers earn up to seven paid sick days a year they can use for themselves or a sick family member.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any of the three House committees it was referred to, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would require most employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to about seven days a year. Workers could use that time when they are sick, need medical care, need to care for a sick family member, or need time off related to domestic violence or stalking. Employers with existing paid leave policies that are at least as generous would not have to change anything. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any House committee before Congress ended, so it never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who currently have no paid sick leave would gain the ability to earn up to 56 hours (about seven days) of paid time off per year at their regular rate of pay. The bill covers employees of businesses with 15 or more workers, plus federal, state, and congressional employees, and it protects workers from retaliation for using the time. Workers at smaller businesses would get 56 hours of unpaid sick time instead. People escaping domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking could use the time for medical care, relocation, or court.

how_it_helps.text: Workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours (about seven days) per year, usable for their own illness, medical care, or preventive care.
The time can also be used to care for a child, parent, spouse, or domestic partner who is sick or needs medical care.
It covers time off needed to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, including seeking medical attention, counseling, relocation, or court proceedings.
Employers may not retaliate against, discipline, or count sick leave against workers under attendance policies, and workers or the Labor Department can sue to recover lost pay plus damages.
Businesses that already offer paid leave meeting the bill's requirements are not required to add anything more.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost of providing the paid leave, capped at 56 hours per employee per year, plus recordkeeping and posting requirements. Businesses with fewer than 15 employees could substitute unpaid time, limiting their cost. The cost falls hardest on industries that employ many low-wage hourly workers without existing sick leave benefits.

drawbacks.text: Employers, especially small and low-margin businesses, would bear the cost of up to seven paid days per employee per year, and the bill offers no federal subsidy or tax offset to cover it.
Businesses with fewer than 15 employees get only unpaid sick time, so the lowest-paid workers at the smallest shops would gain time off but no pay.
Employers may require a doctor's note for absences longer than three consecutive workdays, a cost and hurdle for workers without easy access to health care.
The bill does not require paying out unused sick time when a worker leaves a job, so unused hours have no cash value.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: paid sick time reduces the choice between losing wages and working sick, and coverage for the worker's own illness and family care reaches a large share of the workforce. The strongest good-faith objections are real: businesses bear payroll costs, and small firms under 15 employees get only unpaid time, which may not be usable by the lowest-paid workers it targets. The 56-hour cap, the no-cashout rule, and the employer-friendly scheduling and certification rules temper the burden considerably, but the requirement is still a genuine mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees, but none of them ever held a hearing or voted on it, so it died quietly when the two-year congressional session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Healthy Families Act on May 17, 2023, in the 118th Congress.
The same day, the House referred it to three committees: Education and the Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight and Accountability.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill had 134 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support in the record.
Congress.gov records the bill's final status as it stood at the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who do not currently provide paid sick leave avoided a new payroll mandate. Millions of workers who lack paid sick days gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 17, 2023 and remained its lead sponsor.

for.name: 134 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a majority-Democrat show of support in the House.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without holding a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

against.name: House Oversight and Accountability Committee and House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 134 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on; Republicans controlled the House and its committees, which took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Employers without existing paid sick leave (retail, food service, hospitality, caregiving)
industries.note: These employers would bear the cost of up to seven paid sick days per employee per year, a direct payroll expense. The industries most affected are those with many low-wage, hourly workers and the least existing leave.

industries.industry: Employers with generous existing paid leave
industries.note: Companies that already offer equivalent paid leave would owe nothing new under the bill, so large firms with existing benefits are largely untouched while smaller competitors face a new mandate.

industries.industry: Federal and state governments (as large employers and enforcers)
industries.note: The bill applies to public agencies and federal offices as employers, adding the same obligation for their workers.
